title: Exact Euclidean SVP in single-exponential time and polynomial space
formal: Do absolute constants \(C,d>0\) and a randomized classical algorithm exist that, given any rational rank-n lattice basis B of bit length L, find a shortest nonzero Euclidean lattice vector with probability at least \(2/3\) using at most \(2^{Cn}\mathrm{L}^{d}\) bit operations and \(\mathrm{L}^{d}\) bits of working space?
definitions: The input is \(B\in Q^{m\times n}\), with \(m\ge n\ge 1\) and linearly independent columns; each rational entry is encoded by a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. L includes the matrix dimensions and all entry encodings. The lattice is \(\Lambda (B)=\{Bz:z\in Z^{n}\}\), and \(\lambda _{1}(\Lambda )=\min\)_{\(z\in Z^{n}\)\{0}}\(\Vert Bz\Vert _{2}\), with the ordinary Euclidean norm in \(R^{m}\). Output a nonzero integer coordinate vector z satisfying \(\Vert Bz\Vert _{2}=\lambda _{1}(\Lambda )\); any minimizer is acceptable. The algorithm is a uniform probabilistic Turing machine with read-only input, write-only output and a stream of independent random bits. Every stored bit, including retained randomness and intermediate lattice vectors, counts toward space; external writable storage and preprocessing oracles are unavailable. The time and space limits must hold on every execution, and the success probability must hold separately for every valid input. The exponent n is lattice rank, not ambient dimension or coefficient precision. All preprocessing and precision management count. There is no promise of a unique shortest vector, a random lattice, a reduced input basis or approximation slack.
answer_criterion: An affirmative answer gives an algorithm satisfying both bounds simultaneously with a proof of exact success on every lattice. A negative answer proves that every randomized polynomial-space algorithm fails some single-exponential-time requirement, or establishes an appropriate time-space lower bound excluding the stated constants. An example defeating one enumeration or sieving method is not enough. Exponential-space algorithms and polynomial-space algorithms taking \(2^{\Theta (n \log  n)}\) time leave the question open.
why: A canonical time-space tradeoff question in exact algorithms: can the single-exponential speed of lattice sieving and Voronoi methods be achieved with only polynomial memory?

importance.reason: A longstanding resource boundary for exact lattice algorithms, central to enumeration versus sieving and increasingly relevant to lattice time-space hardness assumptions.

progress.text: Kannan obtains exact lattice algorithms using \(n^{O(n)}\) time and polynomial space.
Ajtai–Kumar–Sivakumar obtain randomized single-exponential-time SVP with exponential space, as described in the inherited paper.
Hanrot–Stehlé sharpen the enumeration analysis to \(n^{n/(2e)+o(n)}\) for SVP, retaining polynomial space.
Micciancio–Voulgaris establish deterministic Voronoi-cell algorithms; the March 2012 revision gives roughly \(2^{2n}\) time and \(2^{n}\) space, followed by the SIAM journal publication.
Micciancio–Walter reduce enumeration preprocessing overhead while retaining the \(n^{O(n)}\) time scale.

Koyuncu–Linker–Ozel discuss a coarse-grained polynomial-memory sieving regime; a general exact-success and single-exponential-time guarantee for that regime is not established in the inspected analysis.
Albrecht–Lai–Postlethwaite connect hinted-ISIS algorithms to polynomial-memory single-exponential algorithms for broader lattice tasks, relying on rather than proving time-space hardness.

status_note: Open for exact Euclidean SVP with the simultaneous worst-case time and space bounds stated here, following primary literature checked through 11 September 2026. The 2026 sheaf-based proposal discusses a memory-saving regime but does not establish the required uniform exact-success and runtime theorem. Cryptographic time-space hardness is an assumption, not an unconditional negative resolution.

context_blocks.text: The familiar exact algorithms offer two different resource profiles. Enumeration explores candidate lattice vectors while retaining a relatively small search state, but its proved worst-case time is \(n^{O(n)}\). Sieving and Voronoi methods achieve \(2^{O(n)}\) time by retaining exponentially many vectors or geometric constraints. The question asks whether one can obtain the faster asymptotic time without the exponential memory.

These time scales differ by more than a constant in the exponent: \(n^{cn}=2^{cn \log _{2}n}\). For any fixed C, the factor \(\log _{2}n\) eventually makes \(n^{cn}\) exceed \(2^{Cn}\). Conversely, this card permits a large constant C. A polynomial-memory algorithm with time \(2^{100n}\) would resolve the existence question affirmatively even if it were unusable in practice and slower than current exponential-memory algorithms at moderate ranks.

The output is exact, and the zero vector is excluded. Returning a vector whose length is within a fixed or polynomial factor of optimum solves a different task. Ties create no ambiguity: if several shortest vectors exist, any one is valid. Rational input also allows exact comparison of squared lengths, so the definition does not rely on floating-point tolerance or an unspecified geometric oracle.

The standard basis illustrates why practical performance alone says little about the general bound. For \(B=I, a\) shortest vector is immediately visible. A basis with long, strongly correlated columns may describe a lattice with much shorter integer combinations. Preprocessing can improve the basis substantially, but its own running time and memory must be charged. Supplying an already ideal basis would remove part of the problem.

Kannan’s enumeration method uses recursive preprocessing to control the search region. Hanrot–Stehlé’s analysis gives the more precise \(n^{n/(2e)+o(n)}\) time benchmark, up to polynomial input-size factors, and later work reduces preprocessing overhead. This refines the constant multiplying n log n; it does not change that scale to \(O(n)\). The bound is about the method, not an unconditional lower bound on every polynomial-space algorithm.

The inherited Micciancio–Voulgaris paper proves a different landmark: deterministic single-exponential algorithms using Voronoi-cell computations. Its March 2012 revision improves the bound to roughly \(2^{2n}\) time and \(2^{n}\) space, suppressing polynomial factors. The paper explicitly leaves single-exponential time with polynomial space as an open direction. Reading only the phrase deterministic single exponential in its title would miss the resource that remains unresolved.

Exponential memory can encode reusable relationships among many short vectors. Recomputing a discarded value may save space, but repeated recomputation can increase the running time beyond the allowed bound. A valid positive solution must control this global cost as well as the size of each local calculation. Streaming a large list through a small buffer is not sufficient if later steps require repeatedly reconstructing most of the list.

Theoretical and heuristic guarantees also need separation. Pruning an enumeration tree or keeping a smaller sieve pool may work well on tested lattices. A proof for the present question must additionally show that the retained search process reaches an exact minimizer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input within the stated time. Successful benchmark instances cannot supply that universal guarantee.

A January 2026 paper by Koyuncu–Linker–Ozel proposes a sheaf-based sieving framework and discusses polynomial memory under coarse graining. Its §4 initially gives storage \(O((M+K)n)\) for M initial vectors and K iterations, then suggests reducing memory when most new vectors replace old ones. It does not provide a uniform proof that this replacement regime retains the exact-success guarantee and a \(2^{O(n)}\) iteration bound on every lattice. It is therefore recorded as a related proposal rather than a resolution of this precise question.

The resource gap is also used in current cryptographic research. Albrecht–Lai–Postlethwaite’s CRYPTO 2026 work derives consequences from hypothetical algorithms for hinted inhomogeneous short-integer solutions, connecting them to single-exponential algorithms with polynomial memory for broader worst-case lattice tasks. Its hardness conclusions rely on a time-space assumption; they do not prove that such algorithms are impossible.

The importance of the problem is that it isolates memory as a potential source of exponential speedups in exact geometry. A solution could change the theoretical basis for choosing between enumeration and large-pool methods. Its cryptographic consequences would still have to be assessed through the relevant reductions and concrete parameters; the existence of some \(2^{Cn}\)-time exact solver is not itself a polynomial-time attack.

sentences: Exact Euclidean SVP asks for a shortest nonzero vector in a lattice given by a rational basis.
The question seeks single-exponential time in the rank together with polynomial working space.
Known fast approaches retain exponentially much geometric information, while small-memory enumeration has a larger worst-case time scale.
Combining both resources would clarify whether memory is essential to the strongest exact lattice algorithms.
The saved review requires every stored bit and all recomputation to count, and does not treat heuristic memory reductions or unverified framework proposals as a proof of the universal guarantee.
